name: Omkareshwar Temple, Mandhata
deity: Shiva as Omkareshwara, Lord of the sacred syllable Om, worshipped together with Mamleshwar (Amareshwar) on the river's south bank
period: A sacred island of the Narmada; prominent under the Paramara kings from the 11th century
summary: On Mandhata, an island in the Narmada said to be shaped like the sacred syllable Om, Shiva is worshipped as Omkareshwara — one of the twelve Jyotirlingas, honoured together with Mamleshwar across the river.

sections.history: The Dvadasha Jyotirlinga Stotram names "Omkara with Amaleshvara" among the twelve Jyotirlingas, and both are honoured here: Omkareshwar on Mandhata island and Mamleshwar, also called Amareshwar, on the Narmada's south bank, so that pilgrims seek darshan of the two together. The island rose to prominence under the Paramara kings of Malwa; a record of Jayasimha I, of the 11th century, already names the Amareshvara linga. Later the Holkar rulers of Indore cared for the shrines. Tradition also holds that the young Adi Shankara found his guru, Govinda Bhagavatpada, in a cave here, and a towering image of the teacher now stands on the island's hilltop.
sections.architecture: The Omkareshwar temple rises on the island's riverward slope in the Nagara manner, its spired sanctum and pillared halls stacked against the hillside above the bathing ghats. The linga is an uncarved natural form, kept moist with offerings of Narmada water. Across the river, the Mamleshwar group gathers older carved shrines within its own enclosure. Bridges and boats link the island to the town, and a path circles the island for those who make its parikrama.
sections.legends: One legend tells that the Vindhya mountain, longing for greatness, worshipped Shiva here with a sacred diagram and a linga shaped from sand and clay; pleased, Shiva appeared in two forms, Omkareshwara and Amaleshwara, and granted the mountain's wish. Another tells of King Mandhata of the Ikshvaku line, who performed austerities on this island until Shiva revealed himself as a Jyotirlinga; the island has borne the king's name ever since. Seen from above, the island's outline is said to echo the syllable Om.
sections.festivals: Maha Shivaratri draws great crowds to both banks, and the Mondays of Shravan are kept with special devotion. At Kartik Purnima pilgrims bathe in the Narmada and light lamps on its waters. Those walking the long Narmada parikrama often pause here. Confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Arrive by the bridge or a small boat, and the temple appears stacked above the green river with the ghats crowded below. After darshan of Omkareshwar, cross to Mamleshwar to complete the pilgrimage. Many walk the island's parikrama path at dawn, passing small shrines, and return at dusk when lamps float on the Narmada.

visit.timings: Open daily from early morning to night, with breaks for worship during the day; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected, with shoulders and knees covered; footwear is removed before entering.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted inside the sanctum; follow posted rules and staff guidance.
visit.gettingThere: Omkareshwar is in Khandwa district, Madhya Pradesh, about 80 km from Indore, which has the nearest airport. The nearest railway station is Omkareshwar Road (Mortakka), about 12 km away. Footbridges and boats connect the town to Mandhata island.
